newsitem.title: CONGO: French troops to quit Congo as peace talks begin.
newsitem.headline: French troops to quit Congo as peace talks begin.

text.p: France was planning to withdraw its troops from Congo on Monday as talks on resolving a bloody political dispute in its former colony were due to start in the neighbouring West African state of Gabon.

The 1,200 French soldiers had helped evacuate more than 5,000 foreigners from the country since June 5 when fighting flared up between the army and supporters of former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
On Sunday, Paris rejected an appeal from President Pascal Lissouba to leave its troops in the capital, Brazzaville, as a buffer force between the opposing factions.
"All the French nationals who wanted to go are gone and the bulk of the foreigners as well," French military spokesman Colonel Henry Pelissier said. "Our mission is accomplished."
"We start pulling out in principle on Monday and that will take something less than a week," he added.
However, France is keeping its embassy open.

"We have not contemplated closing our embassy but naturally we will take the necessary measures to ensure its protection," a foreign ministry spokesman in Paris said. He could not say how many soldiers would stay on to guard the embassy.
The conflict began when the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home in a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a presidential election scheduled for July 27.
The death toll from the fighting could run into hundreds, or even thousands according to some sources.
"The number of bodies in the morgue is uncountable," surgeon Kibongo Nazerne said at the main University Hospital Centre. "It has space for 140 bodies but there are many more than that."

After a two-day lull, fighting flared up again on Sunday when government loyalists rained shells down on positions held by Sassou's Cobra militiamen from the hills behind the city's airport, prompting the militia to retaliate with mortars and tank fire.
Although some Western observers feared the battle would be stepped up around the airport once the French airlift was over, witnesses reported relative calm on Sunday evening.
Earlier, envoys of Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso left on the same plane out of Brazzaville for the talks in Libreville, which will be hosted by Gabonese President Omar Bongo.
"If we did not believe negotiations would work, we wouldn't be going," Lissouba representative Marius Mounbenday told Reuters before stepping onto the plane.
Lissouba appealed for the French troops to stay on in Brazzaville until a lasting truce could be agreed.

"I am making a fervent call. I would have liked French forces, with ourselves and those in the positions opposite us, to have formed a buffer force, to avoid exactly what is going on today," he told French television.

He told Radio France International the election must take place as planned and called for an African peace force to oversee polling. "These elections must take place. Democracy cannot be negotiated," he said.
Sassou Nguesso did not rule out the idea of an outside force. "The international community must organise the elections, check them and ensure security," he told the radio station.
